claims.text: Overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation of the FeNiCrCoCu coating during high-temperature sliding are governed by a uniform nanocrystalline oxide layer.
The oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The oxide layer mediates near-surface dislocation motion through enhanced dislocation climb and dynamic recrystallization.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating is polycrystalline and may exhibit elemental segregation.
Controlled pre-oxidation can establish a continuous nanocrystalline surface oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
The relevant operating regime is oxidizing sliding above approximately 500°C.
The protective surface oxide is likely enriched in chromium and copper oxides.
The oxide layer modifies grain-boundary regions and thereby alters local deformation behavior.
The oxide layer acts as a sacrificial, low-friction sliding interface.
The sacrificial oxide interface minimizes direct asperity contact.
The oxide-induced near-surface changes facilitate dislocation climb.
The oxide-induced near-surface changes facilitate dynamic recrystallization.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have a lower wear rate than untreated coatings during high-temperature sliding.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have a lower coefficient of friction than untreated coatings during high-temperature sliding.
Pre-oxidized coatings will develop a more homogeneous deformation microstructure with fewer localized shear bands.
At lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres, the beneficial oxide layer may not form or may be ineffective.
Elemental segregation may cause variability in oxide formation and mechanical response.
The optimal oxide chemistry, thickness, and uniformity are not established.
A 600°C oxidizing-atmosphere sliding test comparing pre-oxidized and as-deposited coatings can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant wear-rate decrease together with failure to obtain more homogeneous deformation would falsify the hypothesis.
